question: What is Compose Multiplatform and how does it relate to Jetpack Compose?
answer:
Compose Multiplatform (CMP) is JetBrains' build of Jetpack Compose for non-Android targets — iOS, desktop on the JVM, and web on Wasm. The composable APIs you already know (Column, Row, Modifier, Material 3) are the same ones.

Relationship:
• Jetpack Compose is Google's Android runtime and UI toolkit.
• CMP is JetBrains' multiplatform build of the same source, tracking each Compose release.
• On Android, CMP simply delegates to Jetpack Compose — there is no second renderer.
• On iOS and desktop it draws with Skia onto a platform surface.

Maturity, which is the part people still get wrong:
• Android and desktop — production for years.
• iOS — Stable since Compose Multiplatform 1.8 in May 2025. The API surface is frozen, VoiceOver accessibility and type-safe navigation are in, and UIKit/SwiftUI interop works both directions. It is a supported production target, not an experiment.
• Web on Wasm — Beta. Usable, but expect churn and a large initial payload.

Gain: one UI codebase across platforms. Cost: the result looks like your design system everywhere, so anything that must feel platform-native still needs platform work.

question: Where do images, strings and fonts live in a Compose Multiplatform project, and how do you reference them?
answer:
CMP ships its own resource system that generates a typed `Res` object from files in your source sets — it uses neither Android's `R` class nor iOS asset catalogs.

Layout — a `composeResources/` directory in any source set (commonMain for shared assets, androidMain or iosMain to override per platform):
• `drawable/` — images and vector XML.
• `font/` — typefaces.
• `values/strings.xml` — strings in the Android XML format, with `values-ru/`, `values-de/` and other qualifier folders for locales, and plurals alongside them.
• `files/` — arbitrary raw bytes.

Access:
• In composition — `painterResource(Res.drawable.logo)`, `stringResource(Res.string.hello, name)`, `pluralStringResource(...)`, `Font(Res.font.sora_bold)`.
• Outside composition, as suspend functions — `getString(Res.string.hello)`, `Res.readBytes("files/config.json")`, and `Res.getUri(...)` when you have to hand a path to an interop view.
• The multiplatform resources API has been stable since Compose Multiplatform 1.7, so the common accessors no longer need an experimental opt-in.

Everything is packed into each platform binary, so nothing gets copied per target. Large or remote imagery does not belong here — use Coil 3, which is multiplatform and can reuse the Ktor engine you already have.

question: How do you embed a real native view (MapKit, AVPlayer, a WebView) inside a Compose Multiplatform screen?
answer:
Every CMP target has an interop composable that hosts a real platform view inside the Compose tree, so 'we need MapKit here' is never a reason to hand a whole screen back to the platform.

• Android — `AndroidView { factory }` hosts any `View`; `AndroidExternalSurface` and `AndroidEmbeddedExternalSurface` are the camera and video paths.
• iOS — `UIKitView { factory }` for a `UIView`, `UIKitViewController { factory }` for a `UIViewController`, which is also how you embed SwiftUI by wrapping it in a `UIHostingController`. The current overloads take a `UIKitInteropProperties` argument for touch and accessibility behaviour, replacing the older standalone `interactive` and `accessibilityEnabled` flags.
• Desktop — `SwingPanel { factory }` for Swing and AWT components.
• Web — DOM interop is the least developed of the four; treat it as experimental.

The reverse direction matters just as much: `ComposeUIViewController { }` wraps a composable so UIKit or SwiftUI can present it. That is how CMP gets adopted in an existing native app, one screen at a time, rather than as a rewrite.

Keep the embedded view small and leaf-shaped. Layout, theming, navigation and back handling stay Compose's job; the moment the native view starts owning navigation you have two competing back stacks.

question: Which navigation library do you use in Compose Multiplatform, and what must navigation handle on iOS and web that it does not on Android?
answer:
AndroidX Navigation Compose is published for every Compose Multiplatform target now and is the default answer — the old advice to reach for a third-party library first is out of date.

Options:
• Navigation Compose, multiplatform build (`org.jetbrains.androidx.navigation:navigation-compose`) — the same `NavHost`, `composable(...)`, type-safe serializable routes and deep links as on Android. Stable alongside Compose Multiplatform 1.8.
• Navigation 3, the newer back-stack-as-state model, gained non-Android support in Compose Multiplatform 1.10 and is where the platform is heading. Still early for a large app.
• Decompose — component-based and independent of Compose, so it is the choice when navigation state must be shared with native UI or unit-tested without a UI at all.
• Voyager — lighter, screen-object API; fine for small apps, but it is now a third-party dependency where a first-party one exists.
• Native per platform — CMP screens wrapped in SwiftUI `NavigationStack` and Jetpack Navigation, driven by shared ViewModels.

What is genuinely different away from Android:
• There is no system back button on iOS. The interactive edge-swipe is a UIKit gesture, so a `NavHost` has to opt into predictive-back handling or the screen feels wrong.
• Deep links are declared once but wired three ways: an intent filter on Android, associated domains plus a URL callback on iOS, and the address bar on web.
• On web the browser back button and history stack are the navigation surface, and you have to keep them in sync with the nav back stack.
• Process death and saved-state restoration are an Android concern; iOS suspends instead, so `rememberSaveable` guarantees differ.

For a five-screen app any of these works. The platform differences above, not the API, are what actually costs time.

question: CMP draws its own widgets on iOS instead of using UIKit. What does that cost, and when is it a reason not to use CMP?
answer:
CMP does not wrap UIKit on iOS — it draws its own widgets with Skia onto a Metal surface, so the app looks like your Compose design system rather than like iOS.

Things that used to be real complaints and are now fixed, so do not repeat them in an interview:
• Accessibility — VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch and Full Keyboard Access are supported and part of the stable API surface.
• Text — native-feeling selection, the magnifier, and the system context menu.
• Interop and scrolling — UIKit-like scroll physics, and embedding works in both directions.

What still differs from a native app:
• Typography — Material 3 defaults look Material. San Francisco and Dynamic Type sizing are opt-in work you do yourself.
• Navigation chrome — large titles, sheet detents and the interactive edge-swipe back are Compose reimplementations, not UIKit's.
• Controls and gestures — pull-to-refresh, swipe-to-delete, pickers and date pickers behave slightly differently from the system ones users know.
• Anything OS-integrated — Live Activities, widgets, App Intents, share extensions, Handoff — is native code either way.

Reasons not to use CMP:
• 'Indistinguishable from native' is a hard product requirement, as in banking or premium consumer brands.
• The app is mostly platform integrations rather than screens.
• There is little logic to share, so you would pay the tooling cost for nothing.

Where it shines: brand-driven design systems that deliberately look identical on both platforms, internal tools, admin consoles, content apps with custom UI. The usual production answer is a mix — CMP for design-system screens, native for the ones that define how the app feels.

question: What does adopting Compose Multiplatform actually cost you in tests, binary size and day-to-day tooling?
answer:
Shared Compose UI tests really do run on every target, the iOS binary grows by roughly a Skia-sized framework, and the remaining tooling gap is the iOS build loop.

Testing:
• `runComposeUiTest` runs the same `onNodeWithText` and `performClick` assertions from `commonTest` on Android, desktop and iOS. It still needs an experimental test-API opt-in.
• Android keeps the familiar JUnit4 `createComposeRule` path as well.
• ViewModel and logic tests are plain JVM tests — fast, no emulator, no simulator. Push as much as possible down to that layer.

Binary size:
• An iOS framework carrying Compose UI adds roughly 10 to 15 MB compressed: Skia, the Kotlin runtime, bundled fonts. Heavier than hand-written Swift, much lighter than shipping the Flutter engine.
• Android pays almost nothing extra, because it is already Compose.
• Desktop distributions start around 30 MB because they bundle a JRE and the rendering engine.

Tooling:
• IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin are the supported IDEs.
• `@Preview` works on common code in the IDE, and Compose Hot Reload has reached stable, so the desktop iteration loop is genuinely fast. Verifying the real iOS build still means Xcode.
• Debugging spans Kotlin and Objective-C frames; `lldb` works but symbol names are noisy.
• CI needs a macOS runner for anything iOS and a Linux runner for Android and desktop. They are priced very differently, and that difference shapes what you run per PR versus nightly.

The trade: fewer screens written twice, in exchange for a build you have to understand.

question: A CMP project has one `App()` composable in common code. What does each platform need in order to put it on screen?
answer:
Every target keeps a thin entry point whose only job is to host the shared root composable.

• Android — a `MainActivity` calling `setContent { App() }`. Nothing else is different, because on Android this is Jetpack Compose.
• iOS — a function in `iosMain` returning `ComposeUIViewController { App() }`. Swift calls it and either presents the controller from UIKit or wraps it in a `UIViewControllerRepresentable` for SwiftUI.
• Desktop — `application { Window(onCloseRequest = ::exitApplication) { App() } }` in the JVM source set.
• Web — `ComposeViewport { App() }`, attached to a DOM element. This replaced the older `CanvasBasedWindow` API.

What belongs where matters more than the boilerplate. Theme, navigation host and dependency-injection start-up go in `App()` so every platform gets them identically. Anything the platform owns — push registration, the launching intent or URL, permission prompts, window size on desktop — stays in the entry point and is passed in as a parameter or a callback.

That seam is also what makes incremental adoption possible: because the entry point is the only platform-aware code, you can host the whole `App()` on one platform and a single screen on another, or keep a native UI entirely and share only the layer below it.

question: How do you deal with the notch, the home indicator and the keyboard in shared Compose UI — and how does one layout serve a phone, a tablet and a desktop window?
answer:
Compose Multiplatform maps every platform's safe-area and keyboard information onto the same `WindowInsets` API you already use on Android.

Insets:
• `WindowInsets.safeDrawing`, `safeContent`, `systemBars` and `ime` are available from common code. On iOS they come from the hosting view controller's safe-area layout guide, on desktop they are mostly empty, on Android they are the system bars and cutout.
• Apply with `Modifier.windowInsetsPadding(...)` or `safeDrawingPadding()`, and let `Scaffold` handle it through `contentWindowInsets` rather than hardcoding a status-bar height anywhere.
• `Modifier.imePadding()` covers the keyboard on both mobile platforms.
• Draw behind the bars and pad with insets — Android now requires edge-to-edge on recent API levels, and it is the only approach that survives a device with a different cutout.

Adaptive layout:
• Branch on available width, never on the platform. `currentWindowAdaptiveInfo()` and window size classes from the multiplatform adaptive artifacts are the intended input; `BoxWithConstraints` is the primitive underneath.
• `NavigationSuiteScaffold` picks a bottom bar, a rail or a drawer from that size class, and `ListDetailPaneScaffold` gives you list-detail on wide windows and a single pane on narrow ones.
• A desktop window resized narrow should get the phone layout. If your code asks "is this iOS" to choose a layout, it will be wrong the first time somebody drags a window.

Text scaling comes through `LocalDensity` on every platform, so test with the largest accessibility font size before calling a screen done.

question: What can you realistically ship with Compose Multiplatform on the web, and what still hurts?
answer:
Compose for web compiles to WebAssembly and paints the entire page onto a single canvas, which explains both what it is good at and what it is bad at.

Status first: the Wasm target is Beta, unlike iOS and desktop which are stable. It works, teams ship internal tools with it, and the API still moves between releases.

What the canvas model costs you:
• There is essentially no DOM, so search engines see nothing and SEO is off the table.
• Accessibility depends on Compose's semantics being bridged to the browser rather than on real elements, so it is not equivalent to a well-built HTML page.
• Text selection, browser find-in-page, autofill and password managers behave differently from a normal site, because none of those things are looking at your content.
• The initial payload is the Wasm binary plus the rendering engine, measured in megabytes. First load on a cold cache is slow; subsequent loads are cached.

What you have to wire yourself: the browser back button and history, the address bar as a navigation surface, and deep links. On Android the system gives you those; on the web they are yours.

Also keep two things apart. Compose Multiplatform on Wasm is the canvas-rendered UI toolkit. Compose HTML is a different, older library that composes real DOM elements and shares only the Compose runtime, not the widgets.

So: good for an internal admin tool, a demo of an existing app, or putting existing screens in front of a small known audience. Wrong for a public marketing site or anything whose value depends on being indexed.

question: The same shared screen scrolls smoothly on Android and stutters on iOS. How do you approach that?
answer:
Start by ruling out the ordinary Compose causes, because most of these turn out not to be iOS-specific at all.

Before anything else, check you are measuring a release build. A debug Kotlin/Native binary is dramatically slower than a release one, and a large share of "Compose is slow on iOS" reports are debug builds compared against a release Android app.

Causes that exist on every platform and are the usual answer:
• Unstable parameters defeating skipping, so a whole subtree recomposes.
• State read too high in the tree — read it in a lambda modifier instead, so animation does not recompose anything.
• Allocation or real work inside a composable body.
• A lazy list without stable `key`s, or items whose height is measured expensively.
• Images decoded at full resolution for a small slot.

Causes that really are iOS-flavoured:
• The first frames pay for Kotlin/Native initialization and the renderer's pipeline warm-up, so the first screen and the first scroll are the worst it ever looks. Measure the steady state separately from the first run.
• Interop views inside a scrolling list are expensive — each one is a real UIView being composited with the Compose surface. Keep them few, small and out of long lists.
• Blur, large shadows and big offscreen layers cost more here than the same code costs on desktop.

Tooling: Xcode Instruments' Time Profiler and Core Animation show where frames go, with Kotlin frames under mangled names. Recomposition counts only exist in Android Studio's Layout Inspector — which is fine, because a composition problem reproduces on Android and you fix it once for both.

question: You have a shipping SwiftUI app. How do you introduce one Compose Multiplatform screen without rewriting it?
answer:
The unit of adoption is a single screen wrapped in a `ComposeUIViewController` and presented like any other view controller.

The plumbing:
• In `iosMain`, expose a function that returns `ComposeUIViewController { SettingsScreen(...) }`. Everything Compose needs stays behind that one function.
• In Swift, wrap it in a `UIViewControllerRepresentable` for SwiftUI, or push it onto a `UINavigationController` from UIKit.
• Pass inputs in as parameters and results out as callbacks. The Compose screen must not reach into the host app's singletons; keeping the boundary a function signature is what lets you delete or replace it later.

The mistake to avoid is duplicated navigation. The host keeps the back stack; the Compose screen requests dismissal through a callback and the SwiftUI `NavigationStack` decides what happens. Two back stacks arguing produces a back button that goes to the wrong place, and it is the single most common adoption failure.

Seams to check on the first screen: safe-area insets (the hosting controller decides what the composable sees), the keyboard, the interactive swipe-back gesture, and theming — the Compose screen brings its own colours and typography and will not match the rest of the app for free.

The economics are worth stating plainly. The app grows by roughly the size of the Compose framework the moment the first screen uses it, so one screen carries the whole cost and the tenth is nearly free. That, rather than the code, is what decides whether a pilot is worth doing.

A sensible sequence: share the logic first as a KMP module with `StateFlow`-driven ViewModels, then convert one non-critical screen, then watch crash rate, size and startup before going further.

question: Which Gradle plugins does a Compose Multiplatform module apply, and why can a Kotlin version bump break the build?
answer:
Three plugins do the work, and the second one is the reason versions matter so much.

• `org.jetbrains.kotlin.multiplatform` declares targets and source sets.
• `org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose` is the Compose compiler. Since Kotlin 2.0 it ships with the Kotlin distribution and carries the Kotlin version, which retired the old compatibility table where each Compose release pinned one exact Kotlin release.
• `org.jetbrains.compose` is JetBrains' plugin. It supplies the multiplatform artifacts behind the `compose.runtime`, `compose.foundation`, `compose.material3` and `compose.components.resources` aliases, generates the typed `Res` accessors, and adds the desktop packaging tasks.
• Android modules additionally apply the Android Gradle plugin, and get their Compose dependencies from the same `compose.*` aliases.

Why upgrades break: anything that is a compiler plugin or ships klibs is compiled against a specific Kotlin compiler API. Compose, kotlinx-serialization, SQLDelight and KSP processors all fall into that category, and a klib produced by a newer Kotlin simply cannot be read by an older one. Ordinary JVM libraries have no such coupling, which is why a KMP upgrade feels stricter than an Android one.

Hygiene that keeps it manageable: keep everything in a version catalog, upgrade Kotlin and Compose as a deliberate change rather than a drive-by bump, keep the KSP version's Kotlin suffix matched exactly, and read the Compose Multiplatform release notes for the supported Kotlin range before starting.
